quote: Suppose that X = (X_1, X_2, ..., X_n) and Y = (Y_1, Y_2, ..., Y_n) to be two vector of dependent and heterogeneous random variables having lifetimes following the Semi-parametric model with the survival function F̄(x; θ_i), and F̄(x; θ_i), i = 1, 2, ..., n, respectively. The survival function of the second smallest order statistic of the dependent and heterogeneous random variables with the parameters vectors θ = (θ_1, ..., θ_n) and θ* = (θ*_1, ..., θ*_n) under common the Archimedean copula are, respectively, as follows: F̄_{X_{2:n}}(x) = Σ_{i=1}^n ψ[Σ_{j≠i} φ(F̄(x; θ_j))] − (n − 1)ψ[Σ_{i=1}^n φ(F̄(x; θ_i))], F̄_{Y_{2:n}}(x) = Σ_{i=1}^n ψ[Σ_{j≠i} φ(F̄(x; θ*_j))] − (n − 1)ψ[Σ_{i=1}^n φ(F̄(x; θ*_i))]. In the following Theorem, we compare the second smallest order statistics when the parameter vectors verify the p-larger order with common generator of Archimedean copulas in the sense of usual stochastic order. Theorem 3.1. Let X and Y be two vectors of nonnegative dependent random variables with Archimedean copula of common generator ψ. Assume X_i ∼ F(x; θ_i) and Y_i ∼ F(x; θ*_i) for i = 1, 2, ..., n. If the following conditions hold: 1. ψ is log-concave; 2. F̄(x; e^a) is decreasing and log-convex in a; Then, θ ⪰^p θ* implies X_{2:n} ≥_st Y_{2:n}.

claim: Example (unnumbered, p. 10: scale model with EW baseline, Gumbel-Barnett copula)
quote: Next, we will give a numerical example to illustrate the feasibility of the derived results. Example. First we consider the scale (SC) model in the family of semi-parametric distributions, where the baseline distribution is the EW distribution(α = β = 0.9), and according to remark 2, this model satisfies condition 2 of Theorem 3.1. Take (θ_1, θ_2, θ_3, θ_4, θ_5) = (0.12, 0.28, 0.51, 0.62, 0.73), (θ*_1, θ*_2, θ*_3, θ*_4, θ*_5) = (0.21, 0.42, 0.73, 0.89, 0.92) and the generator ψ(x) = exp((1/θ)(1 − e^x)), where θ = 0.2 corresponding to Gumble–Barnett copula. By simple mathematical calculations, we can find that (θ_1, θ_2, θ_3, θ_4, θ_5) ⪰^p (θ*_1, θ*_2, θ*_3, θ*_4, θ*_5) and ψ(x) is is log-concave. Therefore, the above conditions satisfy the three requirements of Theorem 3.1. Based on the above provisions, explicit expressions of F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x; θ) and F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x; θ*) are as follows: F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x; θ) = Σ_{i=1}^5 exp{10{1 − Π_{j≠i}{1 − 0.1 log[1 − (1 − e^{−(θ_j x)^{0.9}})^{0.9}]}}} − 4 exp{10{1 − Π_{i=1}^5{1 − 0.1 log[1 − (1 − e^{−(θ_i x)^{0.9}})^{0.9}]}}}, F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x; θ*) = Σ_{i=1}^5 exp{10{1 − Π_{j≠i}{1 − 0.1 log[1 − (1 − e^{−(θ*_j x)^{0.9}})^{0.9}]}}} − 4 exp{10{1 − Π_{i=1}^5{1 − 0.1 log[1 − (1 − e^{−(θ*_i x)^{0.9}})^{0.9}]}}}. In Figure 1, we plot the survival functions of X_{2:5} and Y_{2:5}. We find that the image of F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x) is always higher than that of F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x). That illustrates F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x) ≥ F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x), for all x > 0. This confirms the result given in Theorem 3.1.

claim: Counterexample (unnumbered 'Example', p. 12: Weibull shape 0.9, Clayton copula)
quote: Logarithmic concavity of ψ(x) is essential in Theorem 3.1, and the following counterexample shows that log-concave cannot be replaced by log-convex. Example. First we consider F̄(x; θ_i) = e^{−(θ_i x)^{0.9}} and F̄(x; θ_i) = e^{−(θ*_i x)^{0.9}}, i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in the family of semi-parametric distributions, Take (θ_1, θ_2, θ_3, θ_4, θ_5) = (0.13, 0.31, 0.49, 0.61, 0.72), (θ*_1, θ*_2, θ*_3, θ*_4, θ*_5) = (0.22, 0.41, 0.71, 0.88, 0.92) and the generator ψ(x) = (θx + 1)^{−1/θ}, where θ = 10 corresponding to Clayton copula. By simple mathematical calculations, we can find that (θ_1, θ_2, θ_3, θ_4, θ_5) ⪰^p (θ*_1, θ*_2, θ*_3, θ*_4, θ*_5) and ψ(x) is is log-convex. Based on the above provisions, explicit expressions of F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x; θ) and F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x; θ*) are as follows: F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x; θ) = Σ_{i=1}^5 [Σ_{j≠i} (e^{−(θ_j x)^{0.9}} − 3)^{−1/10}] − 4 Σ_{i=1}^5 (e^{−(θ_i x)^{0.9}} − 4)^{−1/10}, F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x; θ*) = Σ_{i=1}^5 [Σ_{j≠i} (e^{−(θ*_j x)^{0.9}} − 3)^{−1/10}] − 4 Σ_{i=1}^5 (e^{−(θ*_i x)^{0.9}} − 4)^{−1/10}. In Figure 2, we plot F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x) − F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x) and y = 0, for all x ∈ (0, 10]. We find that the curve of F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x) − F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x) intersects curve y = 0. That means it's neither F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x) ≥ F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x) nor F̄_{X_{2:5}}(x) ≤ F̄_{Y_{2:5}}(x), for all x > 0. Therefore, log-concave cannot be replaced by log-convex.
